title: Should plot holes involving time travel be exempt from criticism?

commenti.body:
I get the point you're making, and I think we should certainly allow it a bit of leeway. If it's clear they've made an internal logic to the film and nothing the time travel does negates that, then yes, I think we should go along with it. 

But if it's all a bit lazy and contradicts itself due to lack of effort, then we're naturally going to call that out. 

The plot hole thing is something vastly overdiscussed now. It's from the rise of YT film reviews which analyse films to the nth degree and think it's funny to highlight every potential inaccuracy. But it's just films, it's just cinema. 

It's no different to someone telling you a story. You don't butt in and nitpick the entire time. You listen to what they have to say. 

Again, if they are lazy or the result of someone who can't be bothered to work around it, then we can call it out. But otherwise who cares?

It's not something that happens only in time travel movies, and in general it is not a big deal for plots to have holes in them. It's revealing about some flaws in the making of the movie when the audience notices it, generally it means they were bored. But if it's only a few hardcore fans who thought over the structure of the story multiple times, then I guess it's almost expected.
[removed]

Time travel films are like any other sci-fi/fantasy films. They should be judged on their internal logic, rather than external/real world logic.

As an example, take 1978's Superman, one of the greatest superhero films ever made. I don't care whether or not any of Superman's powers are plausible, or even possible. When evaluating the greatness of this film, the applicability of science doesn't concern me. What does concern me is whether or not the film follows its rules. Superman's weakness is Kryptonite? Great, then don't suddenly make him immune to it. I can accept that in the world of Superman, things which are possible in its world may not be possible in our world.

The same for time travel films. If you set up rules, follow them. If there are paradoxes, & you can craft a solution based on the film's inner logic, great, but don't cheat. Don't treat the audience like fools.

That all said, in some time travel films or stories, paradoxes are at the heart of what makes them interesting. Particularly in this case, the film needs to take an intelligent approach that respects the audience, & doesn't play them for suckers.

It's not an inevitability. Some movies are more about the fun aspect (back to the future) while others rely on watertight timelines (predestination or primer). Others like Looper are kind of in the middle, so its up to you whether it ruins it or not. But of course i do not think there can be any hard and fast rule of turning a blind eye to any contradictions in the genre. Depends on the movie

You can make time travel work by infinite branching universes so that you aren't interfering in your own past, or you can simply clarify that this a given form of time travel exempts the user from changes to the past. It's not that hard. Most screenwriters just don't bother.

Time travel in reverse, with causality, is inherently flawed.  The appearance of time travel where causality is severed is not.  That is, the idea that if you travel backwards in time, what you're actually doing is traversing universes shouldn't violate causality.

Also forwards time travel is not only possible, but we already do it. 

Aside from this, even where fundamental laws of space and time are being violated, some stories handle it far more intelligently than others, and this is worth exploring always.

A big gripe is usually that people travel in time and end up in the exact same position relative to a particular blob of matter hurtling around the cosmos (earth) when that makes no sense given how fast things are moving.

When the same machine exists at both ends this is mitigated somewhat.  You don't have to be as hand wavy that way.

Ok but the time travel in that 1978 superman has to be one of the dumbest things ever written, I think everyone can agree. It's so over the top stupid that I think it's just meant to be farcical, especially because it's played with such emotion and gravitas.

Also movies that have no respect for reality often have no resepct for their own rules.  If it was convenient to the plot that superman was immune to kryptonite at a given moment, they'd write that in and then do some fantasy gobbledygook ex post facto exposition as to why it was possible.

I don’t think they need to be “exempt from criticism”, per se. But the tendency of casual internet criticism to focus on plot holes and realism above anything else should be questioned, in general. And so with that in mind, I’d judge a story about time travel based more on the story’s characters, twists, themes, emotional stakes, pacing, and so on. Rather than cataloging the plot holes.
Like when he lifted a continent-sized chunk of Kryptonite into space in Superman Returns
I agree with the argument that the spinning the world backwards works as a visual metaphor. You're not supposed to take it literally.
[removed]

I'm willing to forgive all sorts of mechanical fudging, the really weird thing about that third act is that the protagonist realizes he can do it because of the instructions from the father about *what he should never do*, and that disobedience is never addressed or commented on in any way, positive or negative.
Not just that but how it was done.  Flying fast in a circle wouldn't do that.

It's definitely not what's happening in the movie, but I saw a great retcon where Superman was flying faster than the speed of light and began to see the world go backward in time. Then went near the speed of light to go to the alternate future.

>while others rely on watertight timelines (predestination or primer)

"The permutations were endless"

Primer doesn't have watertight timelines. It has divergent timelines.
Thank you

Yeah, it's like attempting to criticize Norse mythology because the world serpent is big enough to encircle the earth but also Thor can pull it up from the sea with a rope and Thor is big enough to fight giants but also fits in one of their hand mitts. It's not meant to be taken on a literal level. I think art that strives for some degree of realism can be held to that standard (to a point--personally I think putting too great an insistence on plot mechanics is a dead end when it comes to any art) but it's *Superman*, the entire point of him is that he can do impossible things--time travel is no more implausible than stopping a bullet or being able to fly.
[removed]

> Time travel in reverse, with causality, is inherently flawed.

According to some interpretations of causality/metaphysics, sure. But this isn’t immutable fact. I wouldn’t say all (or even most) people whose job it is to argue in favor of or against these sorts of things are in consensus on this topic.

This is why so many of them now have a character at some point say something along the lines of "Don't try to make sense of it..."  

That's them telling you that if you do, you'll ruin the fun.

having said that, I do really enjoy the ones that hurt your brain.

I think if a film understands what time travel is and has rules in place, so long as the story follows those rules, it can contain logic that may not be criticized, or flawed. 

Being John Malkovich, for instance, has no logic in the real world, however, in the film world, it made sense. There was nothing arguing for its irrationality within the film, and so it stood as logical. The film was not out to be scientific and there was no real world science. So for argument sake, we can say time travel is fantasy but with scientific jargon to give it credibility.
No, not "according to some". Causality isn't a theory or hypothesis.  It means one thing affects another. It is indeed an immutable fact.

>Time travel in reverse, with causality, is inherently flawed.  The appearance of time travel where causality is severed is not.  That is, the idea that if you travel backwards in time, what you're actually doing is traversing universes shouldn't violate causality.

How does this apply to Tenet?

“Causality” is not an immutable fact, first, because it isn’t even a claim but rather a concept about which many claims may be made. As for whether one thing affects another, that in itself isn’t universally believed and even so would be insufficient to prove that time travel into the past is impossible, which is the very claim in question.

I would suggest a cursory reading of the SEP pages on [causation](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/causation-metaphysics/) and [time travel](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/time-travel/) to learn why and how reasonable, logically-minded people disagree on these subjects.
